temple-literature: The Temple of Literature is Hanoi's premier historical sanctuary, serving as Vietnam's first university with its preserved stone tortoises and Confucian halls. This heritage monument offers a series of shaded courtyards that provide a calm cultural anchor just a short walk from the busy Old Quarter.
halong-cruise: A day cruise through Ha Long Bay navigates a recognized UNESCO seascape characterized by thousands of limestone karsts. Travelers spend a full day exploring scenic lagoons by kayak and enjoying a fresh seafood lunch on board.
old-quarter: The Hanoi Old Quarter Walk takes visitors through 36 historic streets filled with traditional crafts, local food stalls, and bustling coffee spots. Explored entirely on foot, this historic urban area comes alive in the evening under glowing lights near the city lakes.
ninh-binh: The Trang An Boat Ride takes visitors through a landscape of limestone karst towers, flooded caves, and ancient temples in Ninh Binh. Often described as Vietnam's inland Halong, this heritage site is explored via traditional rowboats paddled by local guides.
mua-cave: Mua Cave Viewpoint rises above the Ninh Binh countryside, featuring a steep stone staircase that leads to high rocky summits above karst towers and winding waterways. The vantage point overlooks the river valley and surrounding flatlands, providing an open view of karst boats navigating the channels below.
hoa-lu: Temples marking Vietnam’s tenth-century capital, set among karsts just outside Ninh Binh. A compact history stop that adds context between boat rides and viewpoints without consuming a full day.
hoi-an-lanterns: After dusk, Hoi An’s UNESCO Ancient Town glows with lanterns along the Thu Bon riverside. Pedestrian lanes, merchant houses, and soft night air make this the defining Hoi An experience — free to wander, unforgettable to linger.
ha-giang-loop: A curated day on the northern loop with a local driver-guide — not a second Ma Pi Leng or Heaven Gate ticket. Use the individual pass and village cards to pin stops.
sapa-trek: The Sapa Rice Terrace Trek offers an immersive journey through the heart of the Muong Hoa valley, where centuries-old agricultural engineering meets vibrant ethnic culture. This guided experience reveals the delicate balance between human labor and the rugged, mist-covered mountains of northern Vietnam.
hue-citadel: Hue’s Imperial City (Đại Nội) inside the walled Kinh Thành — Ngọ Môn, Thái Hòa, ancestral temples, and the Purple Forbidden City ruins on one ticket (~200,000đ, typically 07:00–17:30). This card is the full enclosure visit; inner halls are listed separately so you can pin specific stops.
da-nang-beach: Claim a lounge chair on My Khe and watch the light shift over the East Sea. Enjoy easy coastal downtime between Hoi An and Hue.
phong-nha: Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng National Park protects an immense, rugged frontier of primary tropical forest draped over ancient limestone karst mountains. The park serves as the natural jungle setting and administrative hub for some of the world's most spectacular cave systems.
war-remnants: Ho Chi Minh City’s War Remnants Museum presents the conflict through photography, artefacts, and sobering exhibits. Essential context for modern Vietnam — emotional, informative, and best allotted unhurried time.
cu-chi: Descend into the Cu Chi tunnel network that sheltered Viet Cong fighters during the war. A must-do half-day from HCMC: underground passages, jungle camouflage, and a vivid lesson in wartime ingenuity.
mekong-delta: The packaged HCMC-style delta day: canals, a fruit stop, and a late floating-market call. Stay overnight and use the Cái Răng card if you want the real dawn wholesale.
phu-quoc-sunset: West-coast golden hour on Phu Quoc — beach bars, calm water, and soft light. Uncomplicated and restorative; the island’s easiest “must-feel” evening ritual.
egg-coffee: Taste Hanoi’s famous egg coffee: whipped egg yolk foam over strong robusta in a café classic. A short, iconic food ritual that captures the city’s inventive café culture.
train-street: Hanoi Train Street is a narrow residential corridor in the Old Quarter where active railway tracks run inches from local homes and cafes. Visitors gather along the tracks to drink coffee and watch the train pass directly through the tight urban space.
an-bang: An Bang Beach near Hoi An: soft sand, seafood shacks, and a calmer shoreline than the heritage core. Ideal for a half-day reset between lantern evenings and countryside rides.
my-son: Cham temple ruins in a jungle valley near Hoi An — brick towers of the former Champa kingdom. History and atmosphere for travellers who want heritage beyond the Ancient Town lanes.
marble-mountains: Limestone hills south of Da Nang with caves, pagodas, and coastal viewpoints. A scenic half-day climb combining spirituality, geology, and photos of the East Sea.
cat-ba: Cat Ba Island offers a rugged, mountainous escape into a protected biosphere reserve featuring dramatic limestone karsts and authentic fishing communities. It serves as a quieter, more deliberate alternative to the crowded bay cruises, perfect for those seeking deep nature and slow exploration.
ben-thanh: Ben Thanh Market anchors central HCMC — produce, souvenirs, and bustling aisles under the iconic clock gate. A must-do city pulse check; bargain lightly and go early for cooler crowds.
perfume-river: Sông Hương — Hue’s Perfume River — as a boat, embankment walk, or dusk crossing at Tràng Tiền. OSM and maps pin the classic viewpoint on the tomb-road bend; this card is the river itself (the existing boat outing), not a second river listing.
dark-cave: Zip, kayak, and mud baths in one wild combo. An active Phong Nha day that balances Paradise Cave’s quieter awe.
dong-van: Đồng Văn town as a plateau overnight — the same UNESCO karst as the Hà Giang geopark card. Use dong-van-old-quarter and sunday-market-dong-van for the streets; this card is the stay.
fansipan: Ride Sun World Fansipan Legend to the highest peak in Vietnam and Indochina. This 3,143-meter mountain day combines a world-class cable car system, alpine temples, and dramatic summit views.
bia-hoi: Hanoi Bia Hoi Corner is a vibrant, informal social hub where locals and travelers gather on low plastic stools to enjoy fresh, unpasteurized draft beer. It is a quintessential nightly ritual that defines the social rhythm of the Old Quarter.
hoan-kiem-lake: Circle Hanoi’s iconic lake past Turtle Tower and Ngoc Son Temple — locals do tai chi at dawn, couples stroll at dusk. It is the easiest free orientation stop in the city and links naturally to Old Quarter wandering and egg coffee nearby.
hoa-lo-prison: Walk through the remaining French-era prison known later as the “Hanoi Hilton,” with exhibits on colonial incarceration and Vietnam War POWs. Compact, powerful, and easy to pair with nearby Opera House or Hoan Kiem Lake.
ho-chi-minh-mausoleum: Join the respectful queue at Ba Dinh Square for Ho Chi Minh’s mausoleum, then explore the surrounding complex: presidential gardens, the stilt house, and One Pillar Pagoda. Dress modestly, go early, and check open days — closures are common on Mondays and Fridays.
west-lake: Escape the Old Quarter for West Lake’s long shoreline: lake views, Tran Quoc Pagoda on a small peninsula, and Tay Ho’s café culture. Ideal for a relaxed half-day of walking, coffee, and sunset light.
ethnology-museum: One of Vietnam’s best museums: indoor galleries on ethnic cultures plus an outdoor park of stilt houses, tombs, and communal halls. Especially rewarding before northern highland trips, and easy for families.
thang-long-citadel: UNESCO-listed imperial grounds in central Hanoi: archaeological digs, reconstructed gates, and the wartime D67 bunker. A thoughtful history half-day that pairs well with the nearby mausoleum complex.
dong-xuan-market: Dive into Hanoi’s biggest traditional market for fabrics, household goods, and snacks, then linger for night-market street food outside. A loud, authentic slice of local commerce a short walk from the Old Quarter.
hanoi-opera-house: Hanoi’s Beaux-Arts opera house anchors a graceful square near Hoan Kiem. Photograph the façade by day or catch an evening performance — a polished cultural counterpoint to Old Quarter chaos.
quan-thanh-temple: Visit this historic Taoist temple near West Lake to see its enormous bronze guardian statue and quiet courtyards. A short, atmospheric stop that fits neatly between lakeside walks and Ba Dinh sights.
long-bien-bridge: Walk the pedestrian path along Long Bien’s riveted iron spans for Red River and city views. A free, atmospheric stretch of colonial engineering still used by trains and locals — best at softer light.
st-joseph-cathedral: Joseph’s Cathedral is Hanoi’s neo-Gothic parish church, finished in 1886 on the model of Notre-Dame. Free to view from the square; go at dusk when the stone lights up, or time a mass if you want the nave.
hcm-stilt-house: See the mustard-yellow Presidential Palace from its gardens, then enter Hồ Chí Minh’s preserved stilt house: spare rooms, a carp pond, and the working life behind Ba Dinh ceremony. Pair with the mausoleum morning; gardens stay open later.
ho-chi-minh-museum-hanoi: Hanoi’s Ho Chi Minh Museum is a modern lotus-form building of biographical and revolutionary galleries beside Ba Dinh Square. Stronger on story than objects; go when the mausoleum is shut or as the third stop after gardens and stilt house.
one-pillar-pagoda: One Pillar Pagoda is a wooden shrine on a single stone column over a lotus pond — Hanoi’s most photographed small temple. A brief stop on the Ho Chi Minh complex walk; go early before tour groups fill the pond edge.
tran-quoc-pagoda: Trấn Quốc Pagoda sits on a small peninsula of West Lake: Hanoi’s oldest Buddhist temple, a red brick tower, and sunset over the water. Dress modestly; combine with Quan Thanh or a Tay Ho café, not a rushed taxi photo.
ngoc-son-temple: Ngọc Sơn Temple occupies a tiny island in Hoan Kiem Lake, reached by the red Húc Bridge. Halls, a giant turtle specimen, and the classic lake photo — 30–45 minutes, best before mid-morning crowds.
vietnam-fine-arts-hanoi: The Vietnam National Fine Arts Museum holds religious sculpture, folk art, and modern Vietnamese painting in a colonial building next to the Temple of Literature. 5–2 hours; closed some Mondays — check before you go.
vietnamese-womens-museum: The Vietnamese Women’s Museum covers family life, ethnic dress, and women’s roles in war in a sharp, compact gallery near Hoan Kiem. About 90 minutes; a favourite among travellers who find other Hanoi museums dry.
vietnam-military-history-museum: Vietnam’s Military History Museum gathers tanks, jets, and war galleries beside the Thăng Long Citadel. Outdoor hardware photographs well; indoor rooms add context.
perfume-pagoda: Perfume Pagoda is a full-day pilgrimage into the Hương Tích mountains: boat, karst, and cave shrines about two hours from Hanoi. Start early; bring modest clothes and expect stairs unless you take the cable car.
bat-trang-pottery: Bát Tràng Pottery Village has made ceramics for centuries on the Red River, a 30-minute ride from Hanoi. Walk kiln alleys, watch throwing, and buy from workshops — a half-day that pairs with a late Old Quarter return.
notre-dame-saigon: Stand before Saigon’s red-brick Notre-Dame and the ornate Central Post Office across the square. A short, essential District 1 stop for architecture photos before Independence Palace or Nguyen Hue.
independence-palace: Tour the 1960s Independence (Reunification) Palace: period interiors, underground war rooms, and the rooftop helipad. Pair with War Remnants Museum or Notre-Dame for a powerful District 1 history morning.
landmark81-viewpoint: Ascend Landmark 81 for sweeping views across Ho Chi Minh City and the Saigon River. A polished viewpoint experience — go near sunset for golden light over the modern skyline.
jade-emperor-pagoda: Step into one of Saigon’s most atmospheric Taoist temples — swirling incense, carved wood, and a turtle pond in the courtyard. Compact, photogenic, and a welcome pause from downtown museums.
nguyen-hue-walking: Wander Nguyen Hue’s wide pedestrian boulevard from the People’s Committee building toward the river. Ideal for evening people-watching, street photos, and an easy link between Ben Thanh and the waterfront.
cho-lon: Explore Saigon’s historic Chinatown: incense at Thien Hau Temple, herbal shops, and wholesale market energy around Binh Tay. A half-day of local life away from polished District 1.
apartment-cafes: Hunt café floors tucked inside aging District 1 apartment blocks — narrow stairs, balcony views, and specialty coffee. A quintessential Saigon ritual that rewards curiosity more than a fixed itinerary.
saigon-central-post-office: Saigon’s Central Post Office is a living French-colonial landmark: soaring vault, historic maps, and working counters facing Notre-Dame. Free to enter; go early on a weekday for photos without tour-group crush.
saigon-opera-house: The Saigon Opera House (Municipal Theatre) is a French-colonial showpiece on Lam Son Square. Photograph the façade on a downtown loop, or book an evening show if you want the interior.
hcmc-peoples-committee: Ho Chi Minh City’s People’s Committee building closes most interiors to walk-ins, but the French-colonial façade at the top of Nguyen Hue is a must-photograph landmark, glowing after sunset.
tan-dinh-church: Tân Định Church — the Pink Church — is a Gothic Revival parish painted a vivid rose in District 3. A short hop from downtown for architecture photos; check mass hours before entering.
cha-tam-church: Cha Tam (Francis Xavier) Church sits in Chợ Lớn, remembered for Ngô Đình Diệm’s final hours in 1963. A modest historic stop that deepens a Chinatown morning with Thien Hau and Binh Tay.
hcmc-city-museum: The Ho Chi Minh City Museum occupies Gia Long Palace: city history, revolutionary rooms, and a garden pause a short walk from Independence Palace. Calmer than War Remnants, still central.
museum-vietnamese-history-hcmc: The Museum of Vietnamese History gathers millennia of artefacts in a 1929 building next to Saigon Zoo. Cham sculpture and Đông Sơn bronzes reward anyone who wants more than the war museums.
hcmc-fine-arts: Ho Chi Minh City’s Museum of Fine Arts occupies a yellow French mansion near Ben Thanh: colonial rooms, Vietnamese painting, and contemporary work. 5 hours; 30,000 VND typical adult ticket.
nho-rong-museum: The Ho Chi Minh Museum at Nhà Rồng Wharf marks the 1911 departure of Nguyễn Tất Thành from this historic port. River setting, dragon-roof warehouse, and a focused biographical visit near District 1.
southern-womens-museum: The Southern Women’s Museum documents the military and social role of Vietnamese women. A quieter District 1–3 museum hour after War Remnants if you want a second, more specific history stop.
fitom-museum: FITOM, the traditional Vietnamese medicine museum, is cabinets of herbs, old apothecary tools, and a quiet hour off the war-museum circuit. Best if you already have extra time in the city.
vinh-nghiem-pagoda: Vĩnh Nghiêm Pagoda is a large Mahayana complex in District 3, known for its seven-storey tower and busy courtyards. A living temple rather than a museum — cover shoulders and go in the cooler morning.
xa-loi-pagoda: Xá Lợi Pagoda was the headquarters of South Vietnam’s Buddhist movement, marked by its multi-tiered tower. A compact District 3 stop with heavier history than prettier tourist temples.
mariamman-temple: Mariamman Hindu Temple is a compact, vividly painted South Indian shrine beside Bến Thành Market. Five to twenty minutes, shoes off, then back to the market or Fine Arts Museum.
giac-lam-pagoda: Giác Lâm Pagoda (1744) is Ho Chi Minh City’s oldest recorded Buddhist temple: carved wood, courtyard trees, and a tall stupa in Tân Bình. Quieter than downtown pagodas; budget a taxi.
binh-tay-market: Bình Tây Market is Chợ Lớn’s historic wholesale hall: Sino-French architecture, dried goods, and local wholesale energy. Morning only; pair with Thien Hau Temple rather than treating it as a mall.
bitexco-skydeck: Bitexco’s lotus-inspired tower puts you on the 49th-floor Saigon Skydeck above the river and District 1. More central than Landmark 81; go late afternoon for daylight then city lights.
bui-vien-street: Bùi Viện is District 1’s backpacker nightlife street: neon, beer, and late crowds. Treat it as an evening wander, not a daytime sight — and keep valuables close in the densest blocks.
saigon-book-street: Saigon Book Street (Đường Sách) is a shaded pedestrian lane of shops and cafés beside the Central Post Office. An easy, free pause between Notre-Dame photos and Independence Palace.
tao-dan-park: Tao Đàn Park is a canopy of old trees beside Independence Palace — tai chi at dawn, shade at noon, and a short walk rather than a taxi. Use it as a cool pause, not a half-day attraction.
thao-cam-vien: Thảo Cầm Viên, founded in 1865, is among the world’s oldest zoos, wrapped in botanic gardens. Family-friendly and central; combine with the Museum of Vietnamese History at the same complex.
binh-quoi-village: Bình Quới Village restages rural southern landscapes on Thanh Đa Island: water palms, wooden houses, and staged folk culture. A city-side alternative to a Mekong day trip, busiest on weekends.
suoi-tien-theme-park: Suối Tiên is a Buddhist-themed amusement complex in Thu Đức: giant dragons, water areas, and weekend crowds. Plan a half-day taxi from District 1; it is not a downtown stroll.
hoi-an-ancient-town: Explore Hoi An’s UNESCO ancient town by day: yellow façades, the Japanese Covered Bridge, merchant houses, and Chinese assembly halls. Daylight is best for architecture detail before the famous lantern evenings.
tra-que-village: Visit Tra Que’s lush herb gardens just outside Hoi An — walk the plots, learn local farming tricks, and often cook or taste with village hosts. A gentle half-day that pairs well with basket boats.
thanh-ha-pottery: Spend time in Thanh Ha pottery village watching artisans throw clay and trying a simple piece yourself. A tactile cultural outing that balances temple tickets and lantern nights in Hoi An.
japanese-covered-bridge: Iconic 18th-century covered wooden bridge with an ornate shrine inside. Photographing the façade from the bank is free; stepping onto the bridge and shrine uses one Ancient Town coupon (sites ~08:00–17:00).
tan-ky-old-house: Preserved 18th-century merchant house on Nguyễn Thái Học with mixed Japanese, Chinese, and Vietnamese architecture. Family hosts usually give a short tour; flood marks on the doorframe show how high the Thu Bồn has risen.
phung-hung-old-house: Two-storey timber merchant house with distinctive roof beams and carved balconies near the Japanese Bridge. Allow 20 minutes; the upstairs landing is the reason people spend a coupon here.
duc-an-old-house: Historic family house that served as a bookstore and revolutionary meeting point. Smaller and less crowded than the headline merchant homes — a smart fourth or fifth coupon if you like local history.
quan-thang-old-house: Fine example of 18th-century woodcarving and joinery on Trần Phú. A compact stop between assembly halls and the ceramics museum; less tour-bus traffic than Tân Ký.
hoi-an-market: Central market by the river, lined with produce, fabric, and food vendors. No heritage coupon needed — go early for cao lầu and herbs, later for souvenirs.
fujian-assembly-hall: Elaborate 17th-century hall built by Fujianese traders and dedicated to the sea goddess Thiên Hậu. Ceramic dragons, incense, and a deep courtyard — the most ornate of Hoi An’s Chinese assembly halls.
cantonese-assembly-hall: Assembly hall rebuilt in 1885 by Cantonese merchants, known for a grand ceramic dragon fountain in the courtyard. Pair with the Japanese Bridge two minutes west.
hainan-assembly-hall: Historic shrine built in 1875 for Hainanese merchants and sailors. Smaller and quieter than Fujian or Cantonese, with plaques and maritime memory rather than a showpiece courtyard.
teochew-assembly-hall: Intricately carved assembly hall built by Chaozhou Chinese settlers, a short walk east of the main Trần Phú cluster. Google listings typically close around 17:00.
chinese-assembly-hall: Historic shared hall for Hoi An’s broader Chinese immigrant community (Ngũ Bang). Hours can pause at midday — recent listings often reopen around 14:00 — so confirm on the door.
quan-cong-temple: 17th-century temple dedicated to General Quan Công, also known locally as Chùa Ông. Ticketed as a heritage site; Google listings often close mid-afternoon around 15:30, earlier than the halls.
phap-bao-pagoda: Active Buddhist pagoda with traditional architecture and gardens outside the historic ticketed core. Cover shoulders and knees; keep voices low.
hoi-an-central-mosque: Hội An Central Mosque in Hoi An. Visit the simple central mosque used by local Cham and visiting Muslim travellers for daily prayer. A small mosque for Hoi An’s Muslim community and visitors.
museum-trade-ceramics: Exhibition of ceramic artifacts from local shipwrecks and regional kilns, shown in a restored merchant house. Compact, air-conditioned-ish shade, and a smart coupon if the outdoor heat is high.
hoi-an-history-museum: Displays on Hoi An’s evolution from Sa Huỳnh culture to the modern trading town. Next to Quan Cong Temple and the market — an efficient history stop if you like labels more than courtyards.
sa-huynh-museum: Small museum of prehistoric artifacts, burial urns, and jewellery from the Sa Huỳnh culture. On Trần Phú; pair with Đức An or Quan Thắng so the street walk has a purpose.
folk-culture-museum: Traditional rural artifacts, performance arts, and lifestyle displays in a large old house. Often recommended as one of the five coupons if you prefer objects to another assembly hall.
precious-heritage-museum: Photo exhibition and traditional costume collection by photographer Réhahn, highlighting Vietnam’s ethnic communities. Own venue and hours (typically daytime); confirm current entry policy at the door.
kim-bong-village: Traditional carpentry and boat-building village across the Thu Bồn on Cẩm Kim Island. Go by boat or the Cam Kim bridge; workshops are informal — ask before photographing artisans at the bench.
cam-thanh-nipa-forest: Water-coconut mangrove forest on the Thu Bồn river delta. Distinct from the basket-boat activity: come for the palms, canals, and village lanes.
cua-dai-beach: Quiet coastal area where the river meets the sea, east of Ancient Town. Erosion has changed the shoreline — check swim flags.
cu-lao-cham: Archipelago of eight islands forming a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve off Hoi An. Speedboats from Cửa Đại take 15–30 minutes; the season is roughly March–September.
thien-mu-pagoda: Thiên Mụ (Linh Mụ) — Wikipedia’s unofficial symbol of Hue, the seven-storey Phước Duyên tower above the Perfume River. Pair with a boat or Citadel morning.
tu-duc-tomb: Explore Emperor Tu Duc’s romantic tomb complex — lake, pine-shaded paths, and ornate pavilions south of Hue. Allow unhurried time; it is the most atmospheric of the royal tombs for many visitors.
minh-mang-tomb: Visit Minh Mang’s imposing riverside tomb: axial courtyards, twin lakes, and forested hills. Combine with Tu Duc for a half-day of Hue’s finest imperial funerary architecture.
dong-ba-market: Browse Hue’s busy Dong Ba Market for handicrafts, fabrics, and snacks along the Perfume River. A practical local-life stop between Citadel sightseeing and an evening boat ride.
forbidden-purple-city: Innermost royal residence inside Đại Nội (same ~200,000đ Imperial City ticket, typically 07:00–17:30). Heavy wartime damage; you come for the plan of the court and a few restored buildings, not a full palace.
ngo-mon-gate: Main south gate of the Imperial City (same ticket as Đại Nội, ~07:00–17:30). Five portals; the emperor used the centre.
thai-hoa-palace: Ceremonial throne palace inside the Imperial City (included on the Đại Nội ticket, ~07:00–17:30). Look up at the lacquered beams and dragon motifs; this is the hall used for coronations and diplomatic audiences.
can-chanh-palace: Working palace immediately behind Thái Hòa on the Imperial City ticket (~07:00–17:30). Less photographed than the throne hall; useful if you want the full axis rather than a gate-and-selfie visit.
duyet-thi-duong: Royal theatre inside the Imperial City (OSM pin on Road 9 in Kinh Thành). Enclosure ticket plus a small show fee when performances run — typically daytime slots, confirm at the door.
the-mieu: Royal ancestral temple inside the Imperial City (Wikipedia: Thế Tổ Miếu). The Nine Dynastic Urns stand in the courtyard in front — do both as one stop, not two outings.
nine-dynastic-urns: Nine bronze dynastic urns in the Thế Miếu courtyard (Imperial City ticket, ~07:00–17:30). Cast in the 1830s; each urn carries landscapes, produce, and fauna from a region of the realm.
hung-mieu: Ancestral temple to Gia Long’s parents inside the Imperial City (OSM: Hưng Tổ Miếu, Road 7). Pair with Thế Miếu and the Nine Urns; do not make a separate taxi trip.
phung-tien-palace: Restored inner palace west of the main Đại Nội axis (Imperial City ticket, ~07:00–17:30). Smaller crowds than Thái Hòa.
hue-flag-tower: Historic flag tower on the citadel’s south face, free and open in daylight. It sits in Kinh Thành, not inside the Đại Nội ticket.
khai-dinh-tomb: Emperor Khải Định’s hillside tomb (Wikipedia / OSM: Lăng Khải Định, Thủy Xuân). Ticket about 150,000đ; typical hours 07:00–17:00.
gia-long-tomb: Gia Long’s tomb south-west of Hue (OSM: Lăng Gia Long, Tỉnh lộ 7). Allow a half-day with a car; it is not a cyclo hop.
dong-khanh-tomb: Đồng Khánh’s tomb beside Tự Đức (OSM: Lăng Đồng Khánh, Đoàn Nhữ Hài). Separate ticket, often ~100,000đ; 07:00–17:00.
thieu-tri-tomb: Thiệu Trị’s tomb on the Hue–tomb highway (OSM: Tomb of Thieu Tri, QL49). Fits a Minh Mạng + Thiệu Trị west-bank loop better than a Khải Định morning.
duc-duc-tomb: Family tomb of Dục Đức, Thành Thái, and Duy Tân (OSM: Lăng Dục Đức, Duy Tân, An Cựu). Fifteen minutes by taxi from Tràng Tiền.
tu-dam-pagoda: Active pagoda on the south bank (Wikipedia / OSM: Chùa Từ Đàm). Pair with Báo Quốc or Phủ Cam nearby rather than a tomb circuit.
huyen-tran-temple: Huyền Trần Cultural Centre & Princess Temple in Hue. Ride up to Đền Huyền Trân and the cultural centre on the Nam Giao side — dedicated to the Trần princess whose marriage is part of Hue’s origin story, with gardens and a wide city view. Hill temple to Princess Huyền Trân, with a view back over Hue.
tu-hieu-pagoda: Monastery on Đường Thanh Hải, Thủy Xuân (OSM: Chùa Từ Hiếu). Keep voices down — monks live here.
bao-quoc-pagoda: Historic national pagoda (Wikipedia: one of three national temples of Hue). Near Từ Đàm and the railway cutting.
dieu-de-pagoda: North-bank national pagoda (Wikipedia: Tứ Diệu Đế — Four Noble Truths). Emperor Thiệu Trị named it a quốc tự.
truc-lam-bach-ma: Trúc Lâm Bạch Mã Zen Monastery in Hue. Drive up to Thiền viện Trúc Lâm Bạch Mã — a large Trúc Lâm zen campus in the hills toward Bạch Mã, with halls, gardens, and cooler air than the citadel. A mountain zen monastery on the Bạch Mã road.
hon-chen-temple: Riverside goddess temple (OSM: Hon Chen Temple, Huyền Trân Công Chúa). Best by boat from the city or with Vọng Cảnh on the same bank road.
voi-re-temple: Royal elephant temple in Thủy Biều, free or a small donation, daylight hours. Pair with Hổ Quyền (the tiger arena) ten minutes away.
dinh-cat-church: Parish church in the Hue area, free to view from the yard; check mass times if you want the interior. Do not confuse with Phủ Cam Cathedral on Phước Quả hill.
phu-cam-cathedral: Phủ Cam Cathedral (Vietnamese: Nhà thờ Chính tòa Phủ Cam) is a Latin Catholic cathedral in Huế, Vietnam, and seat of the Archdiocese of Huế. Built in almost 40 years (1963—2000) at the site where a Catholic church has existed since the 17th century, this church is one of the largest in Huế. Ngô Viết Thụ’s hilltop cathedral — two towers like an open missal.
hue-royal-antiquities: Royal museum in Long An Palace (same building — not a second outing). Ticket often bundled with Đại Nội or sold at the hall; typical 07:30–17:00.
thua-thien-hue-history-museum: Walk the Thừa Thiên Huế History Museum for Cham, Nguyễn, and 20th-century Hue — a civic collection that sits outside Đại Nội’s restoration story. Provincial history beyond the imperial ticket.
ho-chi-minh-museum-hue: HCM museum on Lê Lợi (OSM: Bảo tàng Hồ Chí Minh, 7 Lê Lợi). Labels mix Vietnamese and English.
le-ba-dang-art: See the Lê Bá Đảng Art Foundation on Lê Lợi — paintings, reliefs, and the artist’s Franco-Vietnamese career shown in a small, well-kept gallery. A riverside house-museum for Hue’s international modern artist.
thanh-toan-bridge: Thanh Toàn Tile-Roofed Bridge (Cầu Thanh Toàn) in Hue. Ride out to Cầu ngói Thanh Toàn in Thanh Thủy — a tile-roofed village bridge from the late 18th century, still the centre of a working hamlet. An 18th-century covered timber bridge in a rice-village canal.
truong-tien-bridge: Trường Tiền Bridge (Tràng Tiền Bridge) in Hue. Walk Tràng Tiền, the 1899 steel bridge linking the citadel bank to Lê Lợi — Hue’s everyday crossing and the city’s night photograph. The six-span French truss that lights up over the Perfume River.
ho-quyen: Hổ Quyền (Royal Tiger Arena) in Hue. See Hổ Quyền in Thủy Biều — the Nguyễn arena built for staged elephant–tiger combats, a rare surviving royal blood-sport ground. A circular brick coliseum where elephants fought tigers for the court.
an-dinh-palace: An Định Palace (Cung An Định) in Hue. Tour Cung An Định at 179 Phan Đình Phùng — a baroque-yellow palace Khải Định built off the citadel, later used by Bảo Đại’s family, with painted halls and a formal garden. Khải Định’s European riverside palace, later a last royal residence.
ngu-binh-mountain: Low mountain south of the Perfume River, free in daylight. The view is the point; the trail is short but can be slick.
ho-thuy-tien: Abandoned aquatic park (OSM: Hồ Thủy Tiên, Thủy Xuân). Access is irregular — guards, fees, or closure without notice.
tam-giang-lagoon: Coastal lagoon north of the city (OSM along QL49B / Phong Quảng). Boat or village lunch trips from ~$15–30.
lap-an-lagoon: Lagoon at Lăng Cô / Phú Lộc, free to view from the road; boat or seafood sheds extra. Combine with Lăng Cô Beach or Hải Vân Pass (listed under Da Nang).
bach-ma-national-park: Bạch Mã National Park (Vietnamese: Vườn quốc gia Bạch Mã) is a protected area in central Vietnam, near the cities of Huế and Danang. It covers 220 km2 and comprises three zones: a strictly protected core area, an administrative area and a buffer zone. The park can be accessed by foot, moped or with a park guide's car. A cloud forest and colonial hill station between Hue and Da Nang.
vong-canh-hill: Vọng Cảnh Hill in Hue. Stop on Đồi Vọng Cảnh for the S-curve of the Perfume River, pine shade, and a café terrace used on every tombs circuit. The classic Perfume River bend lookout above the tomb road.
nguon-dai-river: Seasonal riverbed outing toward Phú Lộc / Bạch Mã. Free; daylight; best in drier months (roughly Jan–Aug, confirm after rain).
thuan-an-beach: City beach / estuary (Thuận An ward). Safer swimming depends on surf and flags — this is not Mỹ Khê.
canh-duong-beach: Cảnh Dương Beach in Hue. Stop at Biển Cảnh Dương — a less developed sand crescent on the Hue–Da Nang coast, used by villagers and a few guesthouses. A quieter Phú Lộc beach on the way to Lăng Cô.
lang-co-bay: Lăng Cô Bay & Beach in Hue. Spend time at Lăng Cô — the beach-and-lagoon commune on Hue’s southern coast, a resort stop on the old pass road and a swim day if you are done with tombs. A hooked bay of sand and lagoon under Hải Vân.
thuy-xuan-village: Incense and hat village in Thủy Xuân, on the way to Tự Đức. Free to walk; buy only if you want to.
phuoc-tich-village: Phước Tích Ancient Village in Hue. Spend a slow morning in Làng cổ Phước Tích — garden houses, a river bend, and a pottery tradition older than the Nguyễn capital. A pottery village of old wooden houses in Phong Điền.
tay-loc-market: Neighbourhood market inside the citadel walls, free to walk, liveliest 06:00–10:00. Eat breakfast here; shop souvenirs at Đông Ba.
ben-ngu-market: Bến Ngự Market in Hue. Walk Chợ Bến Ngự for fish, herbs, and cheap Hue plates on the An Cựu / Phủ Cam side of town — a working market, not a craft hall. South-bank wet market on Phan Đình Phùng.
phuong-duc-village: Phường Đúc Bronze Casting Village in Hue. Visit Phường Đúc, the bronze-casting quarter south-west of the citadel, where family foundries still pour bells, incense burners, and statuary for pagodas. The ward that still casts Hue’s bells, urns, and temple bronze.
bao-la-village: Bamboo village in Phong Điền, about 30–40 minutes from Hue. Free to wander; buy direct if you want a piece that fits a suitcase.
da-vien-island: River island park in central Hue, free, pleasant from late afternoon. Couple it with Tràng Tiền or a boat.
dragon-bridge: Claim a riverside spot for Dragon Bridge’s weekend fire-and-water show — the steel dragon lights up and breathes flame. Free, festive, and the defining Da Nang nightlife moment.
son-tra: Ride the Son Tra peninsula’s jungle roads for coastal viewpoints, quiet beaches, and the giant Lady Buddha at Linh Ung. A half-day escape that feels remote despite sitting beside the city.
linh-ung-pagoda: Stand beneath the towering Lady Buddha at Linh Ung Pagoda on Son Tra, with sweeping views over Da Nang Bay. Free to enter, highly photogenic, and easy to combine with Monkey Mountain viewpoints.
ba-na-hills: Ride one of the world’s longest cable cars up to Ba Na Hills for the Golden Bridge, French Village sets, and mountain gardens. Touristy and ticketed, but unforgettable for first-time visitors who want that iconic hand-bridge photo.
han-river-bridge: Han River Bridge is Vietnam’s first swing bridge, lighting the waterfront between downtown and the beach hotels. Stroll it at dusk; if you catch a rotation night, watch from the bank rather than the deck.
thuan-phuoc-bridge: Thuận Phước Bridge hangs across the mouth of Da Nang Bay on the way to Sơn Trà. Stop for the suspension silhouette and sea air; it is a viewpoint, not a half-day attraction.
love-lock-bridge: Da Nang’s Love Lock Bridge is a Han River pier of heart lanterns and padlocks, lit after dusk with Dragon Bridge in the background. Fifteen minutes of photos, not a destination — go at night.
da-nang-cathedral: Da Nang Cathedral, the Pink Church, is a Gothic Revival parish with a weathercock on the steeple. Free to view from the street; pair with the Cham Museum or Han Market rather than a long detour.
hai-van-pass: Hải Vân Pass is a 21 km ocean-view ridge between Da Nang and Hue. Stop at the summit fort for the East Sea; start early for clearer air and lighter traffic.
non-nuoc-beach: Non Nước Beach is the quieter white-sand stretch at the foot of the Marble Mountains — swim, walk, then climb or visit the carving village. Less hotel-dense than Mỹ Khê; still an easy taxi from the centre.
linh-ung-marble-mountains: Linh Ưng Pagoda on the Marble Mountains is a 19th-century complex on Thủy Sơn, with cave shrines and sea views. Do not confuse it with the giant Lady Buddha on Sơn Trà; add it as part of a Marble Mountains climb.
quan-the-am-pagoda: Quan Thế Âm Pagoda is a Buddhist complex at the foot of Kim Sơn (Metal Mountain). Statues, gardens, and a calmer visit than the cave trail — pair with Non Nước stone carving or a beach hour.
nam-son-pagoda: Nam Sơn Pagoda in Hòa Vang is a sprawling Buddhist complex of lakes, gardens, and ornate halls. Plan a half-day taxi from the coast; it rewards anyone tired of downtown bridges and beach hotels.
cham-sculpture-museum: Da Nang’s Museum of Cham Sculpture is the largest Cham collection anywhere: sandstone gods, altar pieces, and Mỹ Sơn fragments in a riverside colonial building. About 90 minutes; go before the site itself if you can.
da-nang-museum: Da Nang Museum occupies the historic Điện Hải rampart on Điện Biên Phủ: city history, citadel walls, and a quieter hour than the Cham sculpture halls. Combine with downtown bridges rather than a beach morning.
fifth-military-zone-museum: Da Nang’s Fifth Military Zone Museum displays tanks, aircraft, and revolutionary galleries, including Ho Chi Minh material. A 60–90 minute yard-and-hall visit near the river — better for equipment photos than deep curation.
non-nuoc-stone-village: Non Nước Stone Carving Village has made marble sculpture for centuries at the base of the Marble Mountains. Watch workshops, skip the hard sell, and fold it into a Thủy Sơn morning rather than a standalone outing.
han-market: Hàn Market is Da Nang’s two-storey colonial-era hall by the river — snacks, clothes, and souvenirs. A short downtown stop; bargain lightly and go for atmosphere more than crafts.
con-market: Cồn Market is Da Nang’s main indoor wholesale market: produce, seafood, and household goods for locals. Morning only; pair with Hàn Market only if you want both tourist and wholesale sides of the city.
asia-park-danang: Asia Park is Da Nang’s riverside Sun World park: rides, themed courts, and the huge Sun Wheel over the Han. Go in the evening for lights; budget a ticketed few hours, not a free bridge stroll.
sung-sot-cave: Walk through Sung Sot Cave’s enormous illuminated chambers overlooking Ha Long Bay — the signature cave included on many day cruises. Bring grippy shoes; pathways can be damp and crowded at peak hours.
ti-top-island: Climb Ti Top Island’s stairs for one of Ha Long Bay’s classic panoramic viewpoints, then cool off at the small beach below. A short, rewarding stop typically bundled into day cruises.
bai-tu-long-bay: UNESCO-adjacent karst waters east of Ha Long. Book a named Bai Tu Long itinerary, not a “Ha Long” label that never leaves the inner bay.
thien-cung-cave: Heavenly Palace Cave on the same island as Đẩu Gỗ. Usually bundled with the nearby cave; bay ticket extra.
dau-go-cave: Đẩu Gỗ Cave (Wooden Stake Cave) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Climb into Đẩu Gỗ (also written Đầu Gỗ): a large dry cave above the water, traditionally linked to the wooden stakes used against Mongol fleets. It sits next to Thiên Cung on the same island. A high grotto named for Trần-era wooden stakes, beside Thiên Cung.
me-cung-cave: Mê Cung Cave (Labyrinth Cave) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Thread Mê Cung’s narrow passages to a still inner lake — a quieter grotto than Sửng Sốt, usually on selected day or overnight routes. A smaller, twisting cave that opens onto a hidden lake.
trinh-nu-cave: Virgin Cave on the Bo Hòn cluster. Smaller than Sửng Sốt — do not book both expecting two “wow” caves.
trong-cave: Hang Trống (Drum Cave) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Stop at Hang Trống, opposite Trinh Nữ: a high opening where wind and swell can boom. It is a look and listen more than a long walk. Wind in the hollow rock sounds like distant drums.
luon-cave: Luồn Cave in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Enter Luồn at water level by kayak or bamboo boat — a short tunnel into a circular lagoon ringed by cliffs. This is the classic “through the rock” stop. Paddle or row under a low arch into a closed lagoon.
dong-tien-cave: Hồ Động Tiên (Fairy Lake Cave) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Visit Hồ Động Tiên when your route includes it: a grotto-and-lake pocket used on some overnight itineraries, quieter than the Sửng Sốt queue. A cave mouth that opens onto a still “fairy” lake.
soi-sim-island: Soi Sim Island in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Land on Soi Sim for a short sand strip and a ridge path with bay views. Some day boats use it when Ti Tốp is crowded or closed to extra landings. A small beach-and-ridge stop, often instead of or after Ti Tốp.
tuan-chau-island: Tuần Châu Island & Marina in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Tuần Châu is a schist island on the southwest side of Quảng Ninh in Vietnam. Overview Covered by palm forests, Tuần Châu island has an area of 2. To the east and south are two man-made beaches with white sand. The causeway island where many overnight boats actually board.
co-to-island: Cô Tô Island in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Ferry to Cô Tô for a proper island stay: beaches, a small town, and open East Sea weather. It is a Vân Đồn / Cô Tô trip, not a Ha Long junk landing. The far-east island district — beaches and a town, not a day cruise stop.
quan-lan-island: Quan Lạn Island in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Stay on Quan Lạn for Minh Châu / Quan Lạn beaches and a working island town. Access is by ferry from the Vân Đồn mainland, not from a Ha Long day boat. A long Bai Tu Long island with a fishing town and an empty east beach.
ngoc-vung-island: Bai Tu Long beach island. Cát Bà is a different archipelago — do not book both as one day.
mat-rong-island: Mắt Rồng Island (Dragon Eye) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Pass Mắt Rồng by boat — a pierced limestone stack photographed as a “dragon eye.” There is usually no landing; the visit is the alignment. The islet whose hole reads as a dragon’s eye from the right angle.
hon-trong-mai: Free with any inner-bay cruise. Pair with Hòn Đỉnh Hương and Hòn Con Cóc as you sail, not as separate tickets.
hon-dinh-huong: Hòn Đỉnh Hương (Incense Burner Islet) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Pass Đỉnh Hương from the water — a solitary stack used in poems and postcards, often near the inner-bay approach rather than a landing. A single pillar that reads as a giant incense burner in the channel.
hon-con-coc: Hòn Con Cóc (Toad Islet) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Spot Hòn Con Cóc from the boat among the named “animal” islets. No landing; the pleasure is the resemblance and the surrounding channel. A squat karst that looks like a toad on the water.
hon-cho-da: Hòn Chó Đá (Stone Dog Islet) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Look for Hòn Chó Đá among the named islets — a stone-dog silhouette from one angle, easy to miss if you are below deck. A low rock profile read as a dog watching the channel.
cua-van-village: Cửa Vạn Floating Fishing Village in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Visit Cửa Vạn by tender or rowboat: floating houses, a small cultural centre, and aquaculture. Many families have been resettled on land; treat remaining homes as a working place, not a set. The best-known floating community — now a cultural stop more than a live town.
vung-vieng-village: Vung Viêng Floating Village in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Pass or paddle Vung Viêng: fish pens, floating houses, and a less staged feel than the busiest Cửa Vạn calls — still a tourism stop, still someone’s workplace. A quieter floating hamlet used on some overnight and kayak routes.
ba-hang-village: Ba Hàng Fishing Village in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Call at Ba Hàng when the itinerary lists it: a compact floating community, less famous than Cửa Vạn, still part of the bay’s working aquaculture. A smaller fishing cluster — three “rows” of boats and pens.
bai-chay-beach: Bãi Cháy Beach in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Walk or swim Bãi Cháy: a man-made / nourished city beach facing the bay, handy after a cruise, not a remote island strand. The city’s long urban beach under Sun World and the hotel strip.
bai-chay-bridge: The Bãi Cháy Bridge (Vietnamese: Cầu Bãi Cháy) is a cable-stayed bridge on Highway 18, connecting Hồng Gai with Bãi Cháy over the Cửa Lục straits, separating Cửa Lục Bay with Hạ Long Bay, on the territory of Hạ Long city, Quảng Ninh province, Vietnam. It is the first, and at the time of its inauguration, the longest central-line cable-stayed bridge in Vietnam. The cable-stayed span linking Bãi Cháy to Hòn Gai across Cửa Lục.
bai-tho-mountain: Bài Thơ Mountain (Poem Mountain) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Climb or ride up Núi Bài Thơ — the “poem mountain” facing the bay, named for verses associated with Lê Thánh Tông and later visitors. Lôi Âm Pagoda sits on the same massif. The limestone hill over Hòn Gai with a carved poem and a city view.
quang-ninh-museum: Quảng Ninh Museum & Library in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Tour the Quảng Ninh Museum (with its library wing): a contemporary building presenting the province’s mining, seascape, and cultural history. A land day when the bay is fogged in. A striking modern museum on the Bãi Cháy shore — coal, bay, and province.
sun-world-halong: Sun World Halong Complex in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Buy the Sun World Ha Long campus ticket for Bãi Cháy hill — Queen Cable Car, Sun Wheel, Dragon Park, and Typhoon Water Park share one hillside. Inner cards are the rides, not extra destinations. The Bãi Cháy hillside ticket: cable, wheel, Dragon Park, and water park.
queen-cable-halong: Queen Cable Car in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Ride Cáp treo Nữ Hoàng as the main lift into Sun World — bay views on the way up, parks at the top. It is the access, not a separate mountain. The gondola from Bãi Cháy Beach up the Sun World hill.
sun-wheel-halong: Sun Wheel Ha Long in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Ride the Sun Wheel on the Sun World summit for a slow 360° of the city, bridge, and outer karsts. Best after dusk when the wheel is lit. The hilltop Ferris wheel over Bãi Cháy and the bay mouth.
dragon-park-halong: Amusement rides on the Sun World campus. Pair with Typhoon only if you have a full day and a change of clothes.
typhoon-water-park: Swim Typhoon Water Park on the same campus ticket as Dragon Park. Seasonal hours; bring a suit and expect local-holiday crowds. Slides and pools on the Sun World hillside — summer land day.
ha-long-market: Ha Long Market (Chợ Hạ Long 1) in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Shop Chợ Hạ Long 1 on the older Hòn Gai side: a working city market, not the Bãi Cháy night-souvenir strip. The Hòn Gai covered market — produce, seafood, and household aisles.
bai-chay-night-market: Wander the Bãi Cháy night market after the beach or Sun World — clothes, snacks, and bay souvenirs. Bargain lightly; this is not Chợ Hạ Long 1. Souvenir lanes and grilled snacks behind the Bãi Cháy hotel strip.
ha-long-flower-park: Hạ Long Flower Park in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Walk Công viên hoa Hạ Long for seasonal beds, paths, and a calm hour between the museum and the beach. It is a city park, not a botanical expedition. A landscaped flower park on the Bãi Cháy waterfront.
funny-art-museum-halong: Pair with Sun World if you are already on the hill. Skip if you came only for karsts.
loi-am-pagoda: Lôi Âm Pagoda in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Climb to Chùa Lôi Âm on Núi Bài Thơ — a working pagoda with a city-and-bay lookout. Combine it with the poem-mountain walk rather than a second hike. The pagoda on Bài Thơ mountain above Hòn Gai.
long-tien-pagoda: Long Tiên Pagoda in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Visit Chùa Long Tiên in the old town — a late-Nguyễn / early-20th-century city pagoda, easier than the hill climb to Lôi Âm. Hòn Gai’s central pagoda at the foot of Bài Thơ.
cua-ong-temple: Cửa Ông Temple (Vietnamese: Đền Cửa Ông) is located in Cửa Ông Ward, Cẩm Phả, Quảng Ninh province, Vietnam. This is a place of worship for Hưng Nhượng Đại Vương Trần Quốc Tảng, a famous figure during the Trần dynasty, and it is also the venue for the annual Cửa Ông Temple Festival. At the end of 2017, Cửa Ông Temple was classified by the government as a Special National Site. A major coastal temple in Cẩm Phả, east of Ha Long City.
tran-quoc-nghien-temple: Trần Quốc Nghiễn Temple in Ha Long, Quang Ninh. Stop at Đền Trần Quốc Nghiễn in Ha Long City — a local temple to the same figure honored at Cửa Ông, sitting along the waterfront road named for him. The city shrine to the Trần prince who gives the coastal road its name.
bao-bien-road: 45–90 minutes on foot or by xe. Pair with Bãi Cháy Bridge and the Trần Quốc Nghiễn temple.
trang-an-boats: Row the UNESCO Trang An boat circuits through river caves, karst walls, and small temple landings. Slightly more structured than Tam Coc and excellent for half-day photography without motorcycle logistics.
tam-coc-boats: Glide through Tam Coc’s rice paddies and three low river caves on a traditional wooden boat. More village-edge and intimate than Trang An — go early to beat heat and overlapping boats.
van-long: Drift through Van Long’s wetland reserve beneath sheer limestone cliffs — quieter and wilder than Tam Coc. Ideal when you want Ninh Binh scenery without peak-hour boat traffic.
bai-dinh: Visit Bai Dinh, one of Vietnam’s largest pagoda complexes — vast courtyards, long Arhat corridors, and hilltop views near Trang An. A cultural counterweight to Ninh Binh’s boat-focused days.
thung-nham: Ecotourism park in Hải Nham with a bird garden (dozens of species, late-afternoon roost), caves, and garden walks. Adult ticket about 150,000đ includes the boat and Bút Cave.
tuyet-tinh-coc: Secluded limestone valley and cave temple just behind Đền Đinh Tiên Hoàng. Usually included on the Hoa Lư ticket (~20,000đ).
cuc-phuong: Oldest national park in Vietnam (~120 km from Hanoi). Gate about 60,000đ; each rescue centre is extra (~50,000đ).
dong-thien-ha: Galaxy Cave: about 200 m dry, 500 m on water, southwest of Hoa Lư. Typical visit 07:00–17:00 with a combined walk-and-boat ticket.
dong-tien-canh: Compact cave in the Tam Cốc–Bích Động scenic area, often paired with Bích Động Pagoda on foot or by bicycle. Daylight hours; a small local fee may apply on top of the area ticket.
bich-dong-pagoda: Mountain pagoda complex in Đam Khê: lower, middle, and upper halls plus Xuyên Thủy water cave nearby. Named Bích Động in the 18th century.
thai-vi-temple: 13th-century temple to Trần rulers in the Tam Cốc–Bích Động area. Easy by bicycle from the boat pier; often combined with Cố Viên Lầu.
hang-thien-huong: Cave temple about 60 m high in the Tam Cốc–Bích Động area, with a carved shrine to Trần Thị Dung. Daylight visit; often on walking or cycling loops after the boat.
den-tran-hoa-lu: Temple to water-guardian Quý Minh on the south gate of old Hoa Lư, inside today’s Tràng An scenic area. Often reached on a boat circuit.
bai-dinh-co: Historic cave pagoda on Bái Đính mountain, about 800 m from the 2003 “new” complex already on this list. Stone steps, dark and light caves, modest halls.
pho-co-hoa-lu: Contemporary “ancient street” in Hoa Lư city (Kỳ Lân area), with shophouses, lights, and snacks. This is not Cố đô Hoa Lư at Trường Yên.
dinh-le-tombs: Imperial tombs on/near Mã Yên hill in the Hoa Lư precinct. Same heritage zone and typical 07:00–17:30 ticket as the capital temples, but a separate walk.
phat-diem-cathedral: Catholic cathedral in Phát Diệm town, Kim Sơn: Vietnamese temple roofs on European stone walls, 48 ironwood columns. Free to view with modest dress; avoid mass unless invited.
kim-son-sedge: Traditional sedge-weaving villages in Kim Sơn district. Informal workshops, not a single ticket booth — ask before photographing.
ninh-van-stone: Stone-carving village in Hoa Lư city. Workshops are open in daylight; dust, noise, and forklifts are part of the visit.
van-lam-embroidery: Embroidery village in Hoa Lư’s Ninh Hải commune. Some houses offer try-the-needle sessions — agree a price first.
bear-sanctuary-ninh-binh: BEAR SANCTUARY Ninh Binh in Ninh Binh. Join a guided visit at the FOUR PAWS bear sanctuary on the Cúc Phương–Bái Đính road in Kỳ Phú, Nho Quan, where rescued bile-farm bears live in large enclosures. FOUR PAWS rescue centre — not a zoo show.
co-vien-lau: Open-air collection of traditional northern houses (~20,000 m²) by Tam Cốc wharf, added to the scenic area in 2008. Come for a meal and a house walk, not a ruined citadel.
cat-cat-village: Descend into Cat Cat for ethnic village paths, a waterfall, and handicraft shops. This is the easiest cultural half-day from Sapa without a full trek.
sapa-market: Browse Sapa’s central market for local foods, fabrics, and people-watching. Local life between treks — compact and atmospheric in cool weather.
ham-rong-mountain: Hàm Rồng Mountain in Sapa. Climb Hàm Rồng, the landscaped hill just above Sa Pa town — cloud yard, orchid gardens, and a rocky crest that looks back over Muong Hoa. Orchid gardens and a stone “dragon jaw” above the church square.
hoang-lien-national-park: Hoàng Liên National Park is a protected high-altitude wilderness area encompassing the Hoang Lien Son mountain range and the summit of Fansipan. It serves as a critical biodiversity hotspot and the primary watershed for the surrounding northern Vietnamese highlands.
o-quy-ho-pass: Mountain pass on QL4D, about 15–18 km west of Sa Pa. Free to ride; viewpoints and the glass bridge are extra.
muong-hoa-valley: Terrace valley south-east of Sa Pa. Road viewpoints are free; village paths and the stone field have local tickets.
sapa-ancient-stone-field: Walk through the Muong Hoa valley floor to examine large sandstone boulders incised with unexplained prehistoric petroglyphs, fields, and figures. This archaeological site offers a direct encounter with ancient highland history integrated into a living agricultural landscape.
seng-my-ty-reservoir: Séng Mỹ Tỷ Reservoir is Vietnam's highest artificial hydro lake, perched at 1,600 meters in the Hoang Liên Son mountains above Tả Van. It offers a raw, industrial alpine landscape far removed from standard Sapa tourist itineraries.
coc-san-cave: Explore the rugged cave and waterfall cluster at Coc San, offering a refreshing natural escape west of Sapa. Navigate the wet rock formations and short jungle paths for a unique mountain experience.
fairy-cave-sapa: Step into Fairy Cave, the small cave usually paired with Love Waterfall on the waterfall road. Explore limestone formations and a cool corridor on the Ô Quy Hồ circuit.
silver-waterfall: Silver Waterfall (Thác Bạc) in Sapa. Stop at Thác Bạc, the Silver Waterfall west of town — a tall roadside cascade with a short stair to the spray. Often the first halt on the pass. A 100-metre white fall on the Ô Quy Hồ road.
love-waterfall: Forest waterfall west of Sa Pa, often bundled with Fairy Cave. Combine with Thác Bạc on the same road.
cat-cat-waterfall: Descend deep into the valley to witness the roaring Cat Cat Waterfall, framed by slate cliffs and historic water wheels. It marks the lowest, most dramatic point of the Cat Cat village walking route.
cau-may: Walk Cầu Mây, Sapa’s timber cloud bridge — a short span used for terrace photographs when the fog sits in the valley. Different from the Rồng Mây glass skywalk on Ô Quy Hồ. The wooden “cloud bridge” viewpoint — mist under the boards, valley below.
rong-may-skywalk: Stand on a transparent glass bridge jutting out over the sheer drop of Ô Quy Hồ Pass in Sapa. Experience high-altitude engineering and panoramic valley views at over two thousand meters above sea level.
ta-van-village: Valley village ~8–10 km from Sa Pa. Paths are free once you are on the trek ticket or community fee; homestays extra.
lao-chai-village: Lao Chải Village in Sapa. Descend into Lao Chải, the Hmong village on the near side of the Muong Hoa trek, with the widest terrace photographs from the road above. Black Hmong houses on the first big terrace step of Mường Hoa.
ta-phin-village: Explore Ta Phin Village near Sapa to experience traditional Red Dao herbal baths, intricate indigo textiles, and a striking ruined French convent. This rural settlement offers a raw, authentic look at highland minority culture away from the crowded valley circuits.
y-linh-ho-village: Walk Ý Linh Hồ, a small Hmong village used as the gentle start of many day treks before Lao Chải. It offers a shorter descent than Cat Cat, with fewer souvenir stalls and a quieter environment.
sin-chai-village: Visit Sín Chải, a quieter Hmong settlement used as an alternative to the Cat Cat stair, offering a forest-edge experience with homestays and fewer tour buses. Experience authentic village time without the commercial gauntlet found at busier nearby minority sites.
ban-ho-village: Bản Hồ Village in Sapa. Reach Bản Hồ, the Tay (and Xa Pho) village down-valley from Tả Van, used for two-day treks and riverside homestays below the main terrace belt. A lower Tay village — river, bamboo, and a longer trek out of Mường Hoa.
nam-sai-village: Nậm Sài Village in Sapa. Continue to Nậm Sài when a two-day trek drops below Bản Hồ — fewer guesthouses, more river agriculture, and a night that is not on the Tả Van circuit. A farther Tay / Xa Pho hamlet past Bản Hồ.
sa-pa-village: Walk Sả Pả, the village-commune that still farms the slopes beside urban Sa Pa, with lanes that feel like a suburb of the hill station rather than a named trek. A short local loop when you do not want a 75,000đ village gate.
hau-thao-village: Visit Hầu Thảo, a Hmong village on the Muong Hoa rim used as a quieter approach to the stone field and terrace viewpoints. It offers a genuine look at Hmong agrarian life far from the heavy tour bus circuits.
sapa-stone-church: Stand at Nha tho da Sa Pa, the granite church the French hill station built in the 1930s. It remains the town orientation point and Saturday community gathering space.
sapa-center-square: Quảng trường Sa Pa serves as the town hinge connecting vendors, the historic stone church façade, and the descending steps toward the lake. Weekend evenings still carry the lively footprint of the traditional regional love-market crowd.
sapa-lake: Walk Ho Sa Pa, the town lake below the church for a short circuit, cafes, and the first cool-air stroll after the night bus. This small hill-station body of water offers recovery legs before a valley day.
kim-son-bao-thang: Kim Son Bao Thang Temple is the monumental sacred structure perched on the high summit terrace of the Fansipan complex. It serves as the spiritual anchor of the cable car journey, distinct from the town pagodas below.
bich-van-thien-tu: Walk Bich Van Thien Tu, the zen temple cluster on the Fansipan Legend summit with incense, courtyards, and cloud. It is included on the cable ticket and offers a quieter space than the main Buddha platform.
fansipan-buddha: Stand at the Grand Buddha on the Fansipan summit complex — a monumental Amitabha above the temple terraces, reached by cable, funicular, and stairs. The photograph people mean when they say they did Fansipan without the last scramble.
sapa-museum: Visit the Sa Pa Museum for textiles, tools, and a short history of the hill station and the Hmong, Dao, Giáy, and Tay communities around it. Forty minutes of context before you walk into someone’s village.
sun-plaza-sapa: Sun Plaza Sa Pa anchors the town center with its French-colonial arcade architecture and serves as the mountain-railway terminus. Visitors come here to purchase tickets for the Fansipan cable system and shelter from sudden mountain weather.
bac-ha-market: Bắc Hà Market is the premier Sunday highland gathering for ethnic communities in the Lào Cai province. It serves as a vital economic and social hub where traditional textiles, livestock, and local produce are traded amidst a vibrant display of Hmong culture.
coc-ly-market: Cốc Ly Market in Sapa. Go on Tuesday to Chợ Cốc Ly on the Chảy River in Bắc Hà district — a working upland market that still loads goods by boat. Tuesday riverside market — boats, buffalo, and fewer tour buses than Bắc Hà.
can-cau-market: Can Cau Market is a vibrant, high-altitude Saturday gathering for Flower Hmong and other ethnic groups near the Chinese border. It serves as a vital economic and social hub, offering an authentic look at mountain life far from the typical tourist trails.
muong-hum-market: Mường Hum Market is a vibrant, authentic weekly gathering in the Bát Xát District of Lào Cai Province. It serves as a vital social and economic hub for local ethnic minority groups, offering a rare, uncommercialized glimpse into traditional highland life.
cao-son-market: Cao Sơn Market in Sapa. Reach Chợ Cao Sơn on Wednesday in Mường Khương district, often via Bảo Nhai and the Chảy River — a remote Flower Hmong market that rewards a dedicated car day. Wednesday upland market in Mường Khương — the farthest of the set.
sao-beach: Settle into Bai Sao’s pale sand and clear turquoise shallows on Phu Quoc’s southeast coast. Bring shade and go earlier on weekends — it is the island’s most loved classic beach day.
duong-dong-night-market: Wander Duong Dong night market for grilled seafood, fruit shakes, and souvenir stalls after a beach day. Lively, informal, and the island’s default evening social scene.
dinh-cau: Visit Dinh Cau’s seaside temple and rocky lookout for Duong Dong sunsets over the Gulf of Thailand. Free, central, and easy to combine with the night market afterward.
starfish-beach: Starfish Beach (Rạch Vẹm) in Phu Quoc. Wade Rạch Vẹm’s clear shallows — the “starfish beach” on the north-west — and leave the animals in the water. Boats and a dirt approach keep it rougher than Bãi Sao. Shallow north-coast flats where starfish sit in the sand.
long-beach-pq: Long Beach (Bãi Trường) in Phu Quoc. Use Bãi Trường for the convenient west-facing hotel beach south of Dương Đông. The existing sunset card is the evening ritual on this coast; this card is the beach itself. The 20 km west-coast hotel strip — sunset chairs, not powder like Bãi Sao.
khem-beach: Khem Beach (Bãi Khem) in Phu Quoc. Swim Bãi Khem, the neighbouring south-east beach to Sao — similar water, more hotel frontage, slightly fewer day-trip crowds on the public bits. A pale south-east crescent next to Bãi Sao, more resort, still turquoise.
ong-lang-beach: West-coast cove beach north of town. Pair with Cửa Cạn or Vũng Bầu if you are already heading north.
ganh-dau-beach: Gành Dầu Beach in Phu Quoc. Stop at Gành Dầu’s working beach: boats, casuarinas, and a view toward the Cambodian coast. The cape lookout is a separate card a few minutes up. The north-west fishing beach under the cape — Cambodia on a clear day.
vung-bau-beach: Vũng Bầu Beach in Phu Quoc. Walk Vũng Bầu — a wide, quieter west-facing beach that still has space between resorts. A long, less-built north-west bay between Ông Lang and Gành Dầu.
cua-can-beach: West-coast beach at the Cửa Cạn river mouth. Pair with Cửa Cạn Fishing Village (the lanes, not a second beach).
thom-beach: Thom Beach (Bãi Thơm) in Phu Quoc. Ride out to Bãi Thơm on the north-east — long, quieter sand with park forest behind it, not the south-east turquoise of Sao. A remote north-east strand under the national park.
hon-thom-island: Hòn Thơm Island (Pineapple Island) in Phu Quoc. Ride to Hòn Thơm (Pineapple Island) on the record over-sea cable or a boat. The island holds beaches and the VinWonders campus; the cable station and Kiss Bridge sit at Sunset Town on the Phú Quốc side. The cable-car island — beaches, VinWonders, and the south-end playground.
hon-may-rut: Hòn Mây Rút Island in Phu Quoc. Land on Hòn Mây Rút (often split North/South) on an An Thới boat day — the default reef-and-beach stop for snorkel tours. A classic An Thới snorkel stop — two islets, coral, and a lunch beach.
hon-mong-tay: Hòn Móng Tay Island (Fingernail Island) in Phu Quoc. Stop at Hòn Móng Tay, a small sand-and-coral islet in the An Thới chain, usually on the same boat as Mây Rút. A tiny An Thới fingernail of sand — often a second snorkel hop.
hon-gam-ghi: Hòn Gầm Ghì Island in Phu Quoc. Snorkel Hòn Gầm Ghì when the boat skips the busiest sandbars — more rock, sometimes better fish, less beach time. A rockier An Thới stop — deeper water, fewer picnic tables.
an-thoi-archipelago: An Thới Archipelago in Phu Quoc. Treat the An Thới islands as one seascape: the boat-day reefs plus Hòn Thơm’s cable island. The hidden snorkel activity is the typical way to see several in one morning. The southern island cluster — Hòn Thơm, Mây Rút, Móng Tay, Gầm Ghì.
phu-quoc-national-park: Phú Quốc National Park (Vietnamese: Vườn quốc gia Phú Quốc) is a national park on Phú Quốc Island, in the Kiên Giang Province of Vietnam's Mekong Delta Region. The park covers approximately 70% of the island. This park includes land and sea area, protecting oceanic species such as dugong. The forested north — half the island is still park.
suoi-tranh: Suối Tranh Waterfall in Phu Quoc. Walk Suối Tranh, Phú Quốc’s most visited waterfall: ticketed path, pools, and a trickle in the dry months. The easy inland fall — a short forest walk and a swimming hole after rain.
suoi-da-ban: Suối Đá Bàn Waterfall in Phu Quoc. Follow Suối Đá Bàn’s boulder stream for swimming holes and a longer walk than Tranh. A rockier stream walk — more scramble, fewer tour buses than Suối Tranh.
ganh-dau-cape: Gành Dầu Cape in Phu Quoc. Stand at Mũi Gành Dầu, the cape lookout above the fishing beach — the geographic full-stop of the north-west road. The island’s north-west tip — wind, rocks, Cambodia on the horizon.
ho-quoc-pagoda: Hộ Quốc Pagoda (Trúc Lâm Hộ Quốc) in Phu Quoc. Walk Thiền viện Trúc Lâm Hộ Quốc, the large coastal pagoda south of Dương Đông — courtyards, ocean, and a monument-scale Buddha. A seaside zen campus — white halls and a giant Buddha on the south-west shore.
sung-hung-pagoda: Sùng Hưng Pagoda in Phu Quoc. Visit Chùa Sùng Hưng, a historic Phú Quốc pagoda inland from Dương Đông, with a working monastic feel and fewer tour groups. An older island pagoda in the hills — quieter than Hộ Quốc.
su-muon-pagoda: Sư Muôn Pagoda (Chùa Sư Muôn) in Phu Quoc. Stop at Chùa Sư Muôn, a modest working pagoda that locals use — not a viewpoint campus. A small island pagoda named for the monk Sư Muôn.
cao-dai-phu-quoc: Town Cao Đài temple, free from the yard; ceremonies at set hours. Pair with Dinh Cậu or the night market.
phu-quoc-prison: Phú Quốc Prison Museum (Coconut Tree Prison) in Phu Quoc. Walk Nhà tù Phú Quốc (Coconut Tree Prison), the museum on the former POW camp. Wikipedia records it as a major wartime prison; displays are graphic. The coconut-tree prison — a harsh 20th-century site in An Thới.
coi-nguon-museum: Cội Nguồn Museum in Phu Quoc. Tour Bảo tàng Cội Nguồn, the privately assembled Phú Quốc museum of local life, fishing, and wartime objects in a garden compound. A private island-history house — boats, ceramics, and a garden of objects.
ham-ninh-village: Hàm Ninh Fishing Village in Phu Quoc. Eat at Hàm Ninh, the east-coast fishing village used for seafood lunches and a pearl-farm hop, calmer water than the west in the dry season. East-coast pier village — crab, clams, and boats on the lee shore.
cua-can-village: Cửa Cạn Fishing Village in Phu Quoc. Walk Cửa Cạn village for a working west-coast harbour next to the beach of the same name — fish, boats, and a slower street than Dương Đông. West-coast estuary village — boats at the river mouth.
grand-world-pq: Grounds often free in the evening; shows and Aquatopia extra. Pair with Sunset Town / Kiss Bridge the same south-end day, not with a village lunch.
sunset-town-pq: Free to walk; cable and some decks extra. Kiss Bridge and the cable station are pins inside this town — walk them, do not taxi twice.
kiss-bridge: Bridge and sculpture inside Sunset Town (same visit, no second ticket). Do not make a separate trip from Grand World if you can walk or shuttle the south cluster.
hon-thom-cable: Hòn Thơm Cable Car Station in Phu Quoc. Board the Hòn Thơm cable at Sunset Town for the 7. 9 km sea crossing to Pineapple Island. This card is the station and the ride; the island is the landing. The world’s longest over-sea cable — the station in Sunset Town.
vinwonders-pq: VinWonders Phú Quốc Theme Park in Phu Quoc. Spend a ticketed day at VinWonders on Hòn Thơm: rides, aquarium/shows, and park food. Cable is usually bundled or sold next door. Not the Safari, not Aquatopia. The island theme park on Hòn Thơm — rides, shows, a full ticket day.
vinpearl-safari-pq: Vinpearl Safari Phú Quốc in Phu Quoc. Tour Vinpearl Safari, the fenced wildlife park in northern/central Phú Quốc — bus or self-drive loops, not a national-park hike. A drive-through safari on the main island — not the Hòn Thơm theme park.
aquatopia-pq: Aquatopia Water Park in Phu Quoc. Spend a hot afternoon at Aquatopia, the water park attached to Grand World. Separate ticket from VinWonders on Hòn Thơm. The water-park campus beside Grand World — slides, not the Hòn Thơm rides.
khu-cuong-pepper: Usually free entry; tasting and sales extra. Pair with Đức Phát only if you like comparison — one farm is enough.
duc-phat-pepper: Đức Phát Pepper Farm in Phu Quoc. Visit Đức Phát if you want another Phú Quốc pepper walk. The vines look the same; the welcome and shop differ. A second pepper garden — skip it if you already did Khu Cượng.
khai-hoan-fish-sauce: Khải Hoàn Fish Sauce Factory in Phu Quoc. Tour Khải Hoàn’s fish-sauce house: wooden vats, a sharp smell, and a tasting that explains why Phú Quốc nước mắm is a GI product. Barrel halls of Phú Quốc nước mắm — the island’s other famous export.
phung-hung-fish-sauce: Fish-sauce factory, free tour typical. Combine with the night market for dinner, not with a second vat hall.
sim-wine-farm: Sim Wine Factory (Vườn Sim) in Phu Quoc. Taste rượu sim at a Vườn Sim garden: purple myrtle fruit, a short walk, and a sweet fortified wine the island sells to visitors. Rose-myrtle wine — a sweet island tasting, not Bordeaux.
ngoc-hien-pearl: Pearl farm, often free tour; jewellery extra. Pressure to buy varies — walk out if you came for the raft.
paradise-cave: Walk the illuminated wooden path deep into Paradise Cave’s vast chambers. Phong Nha’s most accessible show-stopping cave — no swimming required.
phong-nha-cave-boat: Board a riverboat into Phong Nha Cave’s illuminated waterway, then walk deeper chambers on marked paths. The park’s namesake experience — scenic, accessible, and easy to pair with Paradise Cave on another day.
son-doong-cave: Permit waitlist, not a day ticket. Do not book Hang Én as a “Sơn Đoòng lite” without reading the difference.
hang-en: Oxalis overnight, not a boardwalk. Hang Én is a destination of its own — do not treat it as a failed Sơn Đoòng booking.
hang-va: Hang Va is an extraordinary rimstone-pool cave in Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng National Park, famous for its rare calcite towers rising from shallow water. Accessible only via licensed multi-day expeditions, it requires physical endurance and strict conservation discipline.
nuoc-nut-cave: Nước Nứt Cave is a vital, water-filled passage within the Tu Lan system, offering a raw, immersive experience in the heart of the Minh Hóa karst. Visitors wade and swim through subterranean rivers, witnessing the slow, powerful geological forces that continue to shape this hidden landscape.
tu-lan-caves: Oxalis / licensed 1–3 day trek. Inner cave cards are the same system — do not book Tú Làn plus Nước Nứt as two trips.
hang-tien: Walk Hang Tiên on a Tu Lan itinerary: a large dry passage used on 2-day routes. It is not Tiên Cave at Tràng An. A vast dry hall in the Tu Lan cluster — “fairy” cave, not a town stroll.
tra-ang-cave: Trà Ang Cave is a wet river cave within the Tu Lan system featuring swim-through passages and cold subterranean waters. It offers an immersive, uncommercialized journey into the raw hydrology of Phong Nha's karst landscape.
hang-vom: Hang Vòm is a major underground river in Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng, explored as a technical or long jungle trip rather than a lit visitor cave. Confirm the operator; many town desks will not sell it. A long river cave in the western park — specialist access.
hang-dai-a: Hang Đại Ả sits among the western / Tu Lan–adjacent karsts. It is not on the Paradise ticket. Treat it as a guided expedition stop. A lesser-sold jungle cave — book only with a named operator.
hang-over: Hang Over is a high, dusty dry-cave hall within the Tu Lan cave system in Minh Hóa. It offers a stark subterranean contrast to the active river caves explored on wet expedition days.
hang-pygmy: Hang Pygmy is a compact, dry fossil cave located within the broader Tu Lan cave system in Phong Nha. It offers a quiet, intimate look at the geological history of the region through its dormant formations and dry, rocky passages.
son-nu-cave: Sơn Nữ Cave is a secluded and rugged karst system located within the Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng region, requiring a guided expedition to access. It offers a rare, quiet encounter with subterranean geology far removed from the high-traffic tourist caves of the area.
ruc-mon-cave: Rục Mòn Cave in Phong Nha. Rục Mòn sits off the main Paradise road — a cave-and-forest pocket that appears on some trekking menus rather than the boat ticket. A remote western cave / valley used on longer jungle days.
e-cave: E Cave is a minor karst opening along the rural Phong Nha loops, offering a quiet, uncommercialized subterranean stop for independent travelers. It provides a raw, natural contrast to the heavily managed show caves nearby.
mooc-spring: Moọc Spring is a turquoise karst water source on the Chày River eco-trail in Phong Nha. Visitors can swim or walk the suspended wooden boardwalks through a lush jungle canopy.
chay-river: The emerald water corridor of the Phong Nha region, featuring a prominent zipline, kayaking routes, and the approach to Dark Cave. This river combines high-energy adventure sports with dramatic limestone canyon scenery.
hava-valley: Cycle or ride to Hava Valley for fields, a small river, and farmstays — countryside Phong Nha, not a cave ticket. This is a green afternoon when you are cave-tired.
ozo-treetop: Ozo Treetop Park in Phong Nha. Climb Ozo’s treetop courses — platforms, zip lines, and a jungle play park aimed at families and groups, not cavers. A forest high-ropes and zipline park near the cave roads.
phong-nha-botanical: Walk the Phong Nha botanical and forest garden for labeled plants and a flat hour. It provides shade and names of trees after a cave morning, contrasting with deep national-park jungle treks.
bong-lai-valley: Bồng Lai Valley is a scenic agricultural cycling loop near Phong Nha, featuring rural homesteads, local farm pubs, and dramatic limestone karst backdrops. It offers a classic non-cave day out among rice paddies, water buffalo, and traditional farm life.
duck-stop: Pause at The Duck Stop on the Bồng Lai loop for a farm lunch and the duck pond. It is a café-farm, not a wildlife park.
pub-cold-beer: Drink at Pub with Cold Beer in Bồng Lai — a rustic riverside pub, hammocks, and the postcard countryside beer stop. It is a pub, not a cave.
east-hill-phong-nha: East Hill Phong Nha is a quiet café-hill viewpoint offering sweeping panoramas of the Son River valley and surrounding limestone karst peaks. It serves as an ideal late-afternoon escape above the town.
thac-gio: Thác Gió is an open-air forest waterfall west of Phong Nha town offering a refreshing surface experience after days underground. Visit during daylight hours for a walk featuring rushing water, cool spray, and quiet jungle surroundings.
vang-macaque: Visit the Vàng macaque enclosure used by a countryside farmstay: a fenced troop, not a wild-forest encounter. Keep food away and follow the host. A farmstay macaque enclosure — look, do not feed.
eight-ladies-cave: Pay respects at Hang Tám Cô, a wartime shelter in Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng where eight young volunteers died in a 1972 bombing. This is a solemn memorial shrine rather than an adventure cave.
highway-20-memorial: The Highway 20 Martyrs Memorial honors those who built and defended the strategic Truong Son supply route during the war. It serves as essential historical context for nearby sites along the same mountain road.
ben-tien-ferry: Ride Ben Tien when the river still uses a small ferry: motorbikes, a few cars, and the opposite bank. Schedules follow water and local need.
tram-tran: Tram Tran is a historic way-station and junction on the western park roads of Phong Nha. It serves primarily as a meaningful map point along the wartime Ho Chi Minh trail story rather than a conventional museum building.
phong-nha-park-hq: Stop at the national-park headquarters for current cave status, permits, and the official map. The phong-nha card is the landscape; this card is the desk.
khe-gat-airfield: Visit Khe Gat, a concealed wartime airstrip tucked into the limestone karst of the Phong Nha region. Experience a quiet landscape layered with military engineering history rather than typical cave infrastructure.
phong-nha-market: Shop Phong Nha’s covered and street market on the Son River town grid. Morning is when it is a true local market, while the afternoon is largely half-shut.
po-nagar: Po Nagar Cham Towers in Nha Trang. Climb the hilltop sanctuary of the goddess Po Ină Nagar: red-brick towers built without mortar, a black-stone statue in the 23 m north-east tower, and a view over the river mouth toward the bay. Cham brick towers on a hill above the Cái River.
long-son-pagoda: Free active pagoda on 23 Tháng 10, a short hop from the station. Street-level halls plus ~150–193 steps to the 24 m white Buddha.
nha-trang-cathedral: Free Gothic Revival cathedral at 1 Thái Nguyên, near the six-way junction and the train station. Exterior anytime; dress modestly if Mass is on.
hai-duc-pagoda: Free working pagoda on Trại Thủy with East-Asian halls and a hill view. Wikipedia still lists it with Long Sơn as a main city site.
tong-lam-lo-son: Free (donation) Tịnh Độ monastery at Núi Đá Lố, ~11 km north. The 44 m Amitābha is the reason to come.
chua-tu-ton: Small island pagoda off the north shore. Boat from Hòn Chồng, often casual/free or a small cash fare.
kim-son-temple: Free historic pagoda on a low hill in Vĩnh Ngọc, inland from the beach strip. Tradition ties the name Kim Sơn to Trần Nhân Tông in 1301.
nguyen-trung-truc-temple: Small free temple dedicated to Nguyễn Trung Trực. Do not plan a pilgrimage-scale visit — the famous đình is in Rạch Giá, Kiên Giang.
oceanographic-museum-nt: National Oceanographic Museum of Vietnam in Nha Trang. Walk the French-founded Institute of Oceanography campus at 1 Cầu Đá: specimen halls, live tanks, an underwater tunnel, and outdoor pools on a ~20-hectare site that still does research, not only tourism. Southeast Asia’s oldest marine institute, still on Cầu Đá.
yersin-museum: Compact upstairs museum inside the working Pasteur Institute. Wikipedia lists weekday hours around 08:00–11:00 and 14:00–16:30, closed weekends — confirm at the gate.
khanh-hoa-museum: Central Trần Phú museum in an early-20th-century building. Typically a morning weekday visit; hours and tickets change — check the door.
tram-huong-tower: Iconic lotus/incense tower at Quảng trường 2/4 on Trần Phú. Exterior is free anytime; interior exhibits and hours vary by operator.
do-theatre: Architecture and show venue at Bãi Tiên, ~8–10 km north. Daytime photos are free; evening puppet/life-show tickets often 350,000–600,000 VND.
truong-xuan-gallery: Independent gallery; hours and hanging change with each show. Confirm the current address before you go — Nha Trang galleries move.
tri-nguyen-aquarium: On Hòn Miếu, usually bundled into bay boat tours from Cầu Đá. Island/beach tickets are separate from city museum prices.
hon-chong: Small ticketed cape on Phạm Văn Đồng. Combine with Hòn Đỏ / Từ Tôn by boat, not with Ba Hồ the same morning unless you start very early.
hon-do-rocks: Hòn Đỏ (Red Island Rocks) in Nha Trang. Cross to the uninhabited red-rock islet that gives Hòn Đỏ its name. The geology is the sight; Từ Tôn pagoda occupies the same rock. Come for colour, swimming ledges, and a city-shore skyline, not a trek. A rust-red granite islet 300 metres off Hòn Chồng.
ba-ho-waterfalls: Ticketed eco site ~30–45 minutes north. Dry season can thin the falls; after rain the rocks are slick.
yang-bay: Yang Bay Waterfall & Eco Park in Nha Trang. Spend a developed eco-park day 45 km west in Khánh Vĩnh: Yang Bay (“heavenly waterfall” in Raglai) drops about 80 m into swim pools, with rafts, optional mineral soaks, and forest paths on a large ticketed campus. An 80-metre “heaven waterfall” in a 570-hectare Raglai valley.
